## Anatomy of a Quarto document

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
````markdown
---
title: "Lab: Summary Statistics..."
author: "Put your name here!"
format: typst
---

Text you write, in **Markdown**.

```{{r}}
aid <- read_csv("data/adaptation_aid.csv")
```
````
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
1. **YAML header** between the `---` lines: title, author, output format (`typst` makes a PDF)
2. **Text**: your writing, with simple formatting
3. **Code chunks**: R code that runs and puts its results in the document

<br>

**Run** a chunk: ▶ or **Cmd/Ctrl + Shift + Enter**<br>
**Render** the whole file: the **Render** button
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
~3 min. Put your name in the author line now. Running a chunk shows results in RStudio only; Render runs everything from top to bottom in a fresh session and makes the PDF. If Render fails but chunks run, you probably skipped a chunk or created an object out of order.
:::

# Example 1 · Do more vulnerable countries receive more adaptation aid? {.divider}

A simple, descriptive version of Tennant et al. (2024)

## Load and look

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
aid <- read_csv("data/adaptation_aid.csv")
glimpse(aid)
```

```{r}
glimpse(aid %>% select(-aid_pc))
```

::: {.notes}
~3 min. One row = one recipient country. Point out the column types (<chr> text, <dbl> numbers) and walk the codebook in the handout: where each column comes from. This is the Measure step from Part 1: adapt_aid_musd is donor-reported, Rio-marked commitments, not money spent.
:::

## Build the measure you need

Large countries get more aid in total simply because they have more people. Make a **per-person** measure:

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
aid <- aid %>%
  mutate(aid_pc = adapt_aid_musd * 1000000 / population)
```

. . .

::: {.keyidea}
**Every measure is a choice.** Total aid answers *where does the money go?* Aid per person answers *how much does each person's country get?* They tell different stories. Say which you use and why.
:::

::: {.notes}
~2 min. Callback to "numbers are measurements, not the things themselves."
:::

# Summary statistics {.divider}

Mean · median · spread · groups · shares

## Mean vs. median

```{r}
#| echo: true
aid %>%
  summarize(mean = mean(aid_pc), median = median(aid_pc), sd = sd(aid_pc), n = n())
```

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3.2
#| fig-width: 11
ggplot(aid, aes(aid_pc)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = pal["blue"], colour = "white") +
  labs(x = "Adaptation aid per person, US$ per year", y = "Countries",
       caption = "Source: OECD Rio markers (DAC members, 2020–2024 average); World Bank.") +
  theme_slide
```

::: {.notes}
~3 min. Mean much bigger than median = right skew: most countries get a few dollars per person, a handful get a lot. Ask: which number describes a "typical" recipient? (The median.) The sd is large relative to the mean, another sign of skew.
:::

## Who gets the most? Depends how you count

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**In total** (US$ millions per year)

```{r}
aid %>% arrange(desc(adapt_aid_musd)) %>%
  select(country, sids, adapt_aid_musd) %>%
  slice_head(n = 8) %>%
  mutate(adapt_aid_musd = round(adapt_aid_musd)) %>%
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Country", "SIDS?", "Total"))
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Per person** (US$ per year)

```{r}
aid %>% arrange(desc(aid_pc)) %>%
  select(country, sids, aid_pc) %>%
  slice_head(n = 8) %>%
  mutate(aid_pc = round(aid_pc)) %>%
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Country", "SIDS?", "Per person"))
```
:::
::::

`arrange(desc(...))` sorts, `select()` picks columns, `slice_head(n = 8)` keeps the top rows.

::: {.notes}
~2 min. Same data, two very different top lists. This sets up the CO2 Workshop Questions (total vs per capita), so don't give away more than this.
:::

## Comparing groups and finding shares

```{r}
#| echo: true
aid %>%
  group_by(sids) %>%
  summarize(median_pc = median(aid_pc), mean_pc = mean(aid_pc), n = n())
```

. . .

**Composition:** what share of all adaptation aid goes to SIDS?

```{r}
#| echo: true
aid %>%
  group_by(sids) %>%
  summarize(total_musd = sum(adapt_aid_musd)) %>%
  mutate(share = total_musd / sum(total_musd))
```

::: {.notes}
~4 min. group_by() + summarize() = one row per group. The composition question is one of the five question types from the prompt. Ask: SIDS get a small share of the total but a lot per person. Which is the "fair" comparison? (No single answer; depends on the question.)
:::

# One good figure {.divider}

One question · honest axes · plain labels · a source · a takeaway

## What makes a figure good?

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
1. Answers **one question**
2. **Honest axes**: say when a scale is logged; bars start at zero
3. **Plain-language labels** with units
4. A **source line**
5. A **one-sentence takeaway** in your text
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
`ggplot()` builds a figure in **layers**:

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
ggplot(aid, aes(x = sids, y = aid_pc)) +   # data + axes
  geom_boxplot() +                          # the marks
  scale_y_log10() +                         # the scale
  labs(title = "...", x = NULL,             # the words
       y = "Aid per person, US$ (log scale)",
       caption = "Source: OECD; World Bank.") +
  theme_minimal()                           # the look
```
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
~3 min. Point back to the syllabus: "What does this show? Why does it matter? What can I conclude, and what can I not conclude?" Remind them of the AI policy: they must make their own figures.
:::

## A comparison: boxplot

```{r}
#| fig-height: 5.2
#| fig-width: 11
ggplot(aid, aes(x = sids, y = aid_pc)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = pal["blue"], alpha = 0.3, width = 0.5) +
  scale_y_log10(breaks = c(0.1, 1, 10, 100, 1000), labels = c("0.1", "1", "10", "100", "1,000")) +
  labs(title = "Adaptation aid per person, SIDS vs. other recipients",
       x = NULL, y = "US$ per person (log scale)",
       caption = "Source: OECD Rio markers (DAC members, 2020–2024 average); World Bank; UN M49.") +
  theme_slide
```

::: {.notes}
~2 min. Read it together: the line is the median, the box the middle half. Log scale: each gridline is 10x the one below. Takeaway: SIDS get far more per person.
:::

## A relationship: scatterplot

```{r}
#| fig-height: 5.2
#| fig-width: 11
ggplot(aid, aes(x = vulnerability, y = aid_pc, colour = sids)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.8, size = 2.6) +
  scale_y_log10(breaks = c(0.1, 1, 10, 100, 1000), labels = c("0.1", "1", "10", "100", "1,000")) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Other = unname(pal["blue"]), SIDS = unname(pal["orange"]))) +
  labs(title = "Vulnerability and adaptation aid per person",
       x = "ND-GAIN vulnerability (higher = more vulnerable)", y = "US$ per person (log scale)",
       colour = NULL, caption = "Source: OECD Rio markers; ND-GAIN; World Bank; UN M49.") +
  theme_slide + theme(legend.position = "right")
```

::: {.activity}
**Your takeaway sentence?** Call one out.
:::

::: {.notes}
~3 min. Get two or three takeaway sentences from the room and tighten one together. Watch for causal language ("vulnerability causes...").
:::

# One statistical test {.divider}

Could chance alone produce a pattern this strong?

## Correlation test

```{r}
#| echo: true
cor.test(aid$vulnerability, log(aid$aid_pc))
```

::: {.notes}
~4 min. Read three things: the correlation (cor), the 95% CI, the p-value. We use log(aid_pc) because a few extreme values drive an ordinary correlation, and to match the log-scale figure. Recall from Part 1: the p-value asks "if there were no relationship, how often would chance alone produce one this strong?"
:::

## Comparing two means: *t*-test

```{r}
#| echo: true
t.test(aid_pc ~ sids, data = aid)
```

::: {.notes}
~3 min. The formula reads "aid per person, by SIDS status." Look at the two group means, the CI for the difference, the p-value. A big difference with a wide CI: the SIDS group is small and very spread out.
:::

## What the test can't tell you

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- **Confounding:** SIDS are small, and small countries get more per person. Vulnerability, size, or donor ties?
- **Selection:** only countries that *received* adaptation aid are in the data. Tennant's eligibility stage is invisible.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
- **Measurement:** donors tag their own projects; "significant" projects count in full.
- **Inference:** we have nearly every recipient. The p-value is about chance in allocations, not about a bigger population.
:::
::::

::: {.keyidea}
A small p-value says **chance alone is an unlikely explanation**. It doesn't say **why**, and it doesn't say **how much it matters**.
:::

::: {.notes}
~3 min. Straight callback to the Part 1 recap: confounding, selection, measurement, uncertainty.
:::

## Render to PDF

1. Save the file.
2. Click **Render**. Quarto runs every chunk from the top in a fresh session, then Typst builds the PDF.
3. The PDF opens in the Viewer and is saved next to your `.qmd`.

**If it fails:**

- **"object not found"**: a chunk uses something created in a chunk that is now blank or out of order
- **"could not find function"**: `library(tidyverse)` didn't run
- **"cannot open file data/..."**: the `.qmd` isn't in the folder with `data/`

::: {.notes}
~4 min. Blank chunks render fine. The Workshop Questions chunks are blank too, so the handout renders before they're done.
:::

# Back to your data paper {.divider}

## Which summary, figure and test for which question? {.smaller}

| Question type | Summary statistics | One good figure | A test, if you want one |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Change** over time | Values by year; change from start to end | Line chart | Often none; describe the trend |
| **Distribution** | Mean, median, top 10, spread | Bar chart of top units; histogram | Usually none |
| **Comparison** | Mean/median by group | Boxplot or bar chart by group | *t*-test (two groups) |
| **Composition** | Shares of a total | Stacked or simple bar chart of shares | Usually none |
| **Relationship** | Correlation | Scatterplot | Correlation test |

::: {.activity}
**2 minutes.** Look at your question ladder from Part 1. Which row is your question in? Write down the **one figure** you'd make first.
:::

::: {.notes}
~5 min. Emphasize the syllabus: "A clear graph that answers an interesting question is more valuable than an unnecessary regression." Tests are optional for their paper. Variation reminder: each row needs something that varies.
:::
